reviews.title: Great Concept, Weak Database and Inaccurate Estimates
reviews.text: I appreciate the idea behind Welling — making food logging simple by just snapping a photo of your plate. The concept is smart and could be genuinely helpful. Unfortunately, the execution falls short. The product database is woefully lacking, and the app’s generic guesses for what’s on your plate are often inaccurate. Because of that, I find myself double-checking its work, which defeats the whole purpose of an ‘easy’ tracker. I can’t fully trust the numbers it gives me. I even paid for the one-year subscription and now regret it — it just isn’t reliable enough to justify the cost. If they updated and expanded their database, this could be a much better tool. As it stands, it’s more frustrating than useful.”

reviews.title: Extremely Disao
reviews.text:
This is actually the first time I have bothered to review an app, but the experience was so bad that I wanted others to know and hopefully avoid wasting their time.

I was excited about finding a nutrition app where I could chat both to make it easier to track my nutrition vs. goals and to dive deeper into some of the metrics and how to improve.

The first issue is that the app kept forgetting things already outlined. This memory fade cost a lot of time because I had to keep repeating myself. 

Second, there was an issue where repeatedly it would simply reply with something like “Sorry I can’t find the food you are trying to adjust,” even though I wasn’t trying to adjust anything. I would then just reply “focus” and it would get back on track.

These kind of repeated inputs are what drove the final thing that put me off this product. I was trying to work through how to lower my sodium and all of a sudden I got a message “You have reached your limit of 200 chats for the day.” Mind you there was no warning, nothing I saw when I signed up ever mentioned a limit. This was my first day with the app, and I spent a lot of effort trying to figure out how best to communicate with it, and digging into a lot of questions, but probably half of my chats were trying to get it to correct when it had memory fade or glitched. 

Overall, even within the core product there are big problems. It was significantly off in calculating nutrition from a photo I uploaded. Other times even when I gave it a specific brand of something I ate, it miscalculated the nutritional info.

Overall, like a lot of AI tools this one was clearly rushed to production before it was ready

reviews.title: Not Even Close to Ready
reviews.text:
Welling is a typical food tracking app, but with the entry and search functionality replaced by a conversational AI.  Unfortunately, the AI is absolutely not ready for prime-time, which means having the entire UX built around it is a terrible idea.  It can’t retrieve basic search queries.  It can’t adjust former entries consistently.  It makes terrible assumptions about serving sizes, etc.  

You’re essentially forced to save everything as a favorite meal, which entirely defeats the purpose of the AI.

I will say the interface is very smooth and intuitive.  If you weren’t forced to access everything via the AI, it might be a great app.

reviews.title: Inaccurate and unreliable, but still cool
reviews.text:
The idea is amazing and the ai meal prep feature is neat. However, I’ve found the ai estimations to be extremely unreliable and inconsistent. If you put in the same meal twice, it could give you two different sets of Macros. The app told me that 2 oz of my home cooked meal was 180 calories. I copied the same meal and adjusted for 3 oz and it told me, one extra ounce of the same meal was now 1,600 calories. 
I have to double check and edit each meal, something I thought I’d be doing very little of while PAYING for an app. Hopefully in a few years the technology is advanced enough to keep up with what this company is advertising. A little annoyed I payed for three months. My expectations were too high.

Also, I am recovering from major surgery and not able to log 8000 steps right now, which I have told her multiple times. She always promises to make a note and apologizes, but nothing changes. reviews.title: Paid for a year ($120) and deleted it, so disappointed
reviews.text: I bought a full year sub for $120 and gave it a very serious try - entering everything daily and trying to teach the AI but after so so many errors I’m done as it’s way more work than it should be.  Constantly miscalculating food.  No ability to manually enter steps if you don’t want to link to apple health.  Doesn’t have an app for Apple Watch as well!   But ultimately the kicker for me was the constant mistakes in logging and really poor nutritional advice/guidance.  Useless at best, erroneous advice at worst - constantly making mistakes.  Brought zero value and a lot of frustration.  At this high price tag it’s just unacceptable.  Annoyed I wasted so much money trying to commit to this and teaching the AI for nothing.

reviews.title: Perfect Idea Needing Larger Database
reviews.text: I had been looking for a simple food tracker that allowed me to just throw in foods, approximate amounts, and brands, and it give me calories, macros, and an encouraging word. This app just does that. I find it great for people who have previously had a bad relationship with food or dieting in that it’s simple, doesn’t push numbers at you, and leaves positive words with you even if what you’ve eaten isn’t ideal. My only complaint is that branded foods entered (eg a specific brand of protein bar) show up with incorrect — normally higher — calories and have to be manually edited, and then those edits don’t save, so the next time you eat that same item, it has to be fixed again. I imagine this could be fixed by either growing the data being fed into the AI’s database or creating a way to suggest or save edits.

reviews.title: It’s Like Having a Dietitian in Your Pocket
reviews.text:
**TL;DR:** It’s fast, it’s easy, and it has everything I need. Fantastic work!

Welling is by far the fastest and easiest way I’ve found to track calories. Whether you log by describing your food, using a photo, scanning a barcode, or scanning a label, it is incredibly quick and intuitive. The photo and description features are accurate to the label within 5% in most cases, and even closer if you describe your meal in more detail. The voice-to-text feature makes logging even faster. Its ease of use makes staying consistent less of a hassle, which is the most important thing for me.

My favorite thing about the app is how you can actually talk to it. If I ask how my day is looking so far, it gives me a quick rundown. If I need to know how much more protein I need, it tells me instantly and even suggests good ways to get there. It also gives feedback after you log a meal, letting you know what was great or what could be improved, with gentle suggestions or alternatives.

UPDATE: The app continues to improve with regular updates, and I’m happy to see the team is already working on writing nutrition data to Apple Health. The support team is responsive and open to feedback, which makes me excited to stick with the app long-term.

Looking forward to seeing where this goes. It deserves Cal AI’s spot in the App Store, and I’m confident it’ll only get better.

reviews.title: No trial?
reviews.text: After filling out all of my information with the intention of trying to app for the trial and very likely purchasing an annual or monthly subscription, I was incredibly disappointed to find that there was no free trial at all. I am not going to blindly drop $20 on a monthly membership to test out an app that I could end up not liking after an hour, a day, or a week. yes, the subscription model is unfortunately ubiquitous nowadays but the inability to even test basic features of the app for free/at a discounted rate (ex: I would pay $5 for 5 days) immediately made me delete the app.

reviews.title: Deceptive pricing and poor setup
reviews.text:
First off, the app makes you go through a lengthy setup process, and only then tells you that there is no free version, only a one week trial of the mandatory paid version. This is after putting in all your info like weight, height, dietary preferences, etc. Clearly a hidden design intentionally. 

The setup is also not well designed, making you enter text answers to questions that should be optional, like if you have a special dietary restriction, making you type out “no” instead of just making it optional. 

Doesn’t give a good impression, and it’s bad to intentionally hide the payment scheme of your app until after a significant time investment in hopes that more people will sign up.
